summary: Defines a BGP encoding that distributes traffic flow specifications, which describe a class of traffic by matching on packet fields, for IPv4. Routers can use these rules to filter or rate-limit matching traffic, which is useful for quickly pushing out defenses against attacks. It covers both intra-domain and inter-domain use.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8955 defines how BGP can distribute rules that match IPv4 packet fields and specify actions for matching traffic. Routers validate received rules against unicast routes before using them, subject to local configuration.

subtitle: BGP carries packet-matching rules and actions to routers that filter traffic.

tldr.problem: Static traffic filters are difficult to coordinate when a network needs to react to a traffic flow across routers or providers.
tldr.mechanism: BGP distributes Flow Specification rules that match packet fields and attaches Extended Communities that state filtering actions.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8955 obsoletes RFC 5575 and RFC 7674 and has been updated by RFC 8956, RFC 9117 and RFC 9184.

today: RFC 8955 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5575 and RFC 7674. It has been updated by RFC 8956, RFC 9117 and RFC 9184.

sections.title: Flow Rules Distributed Through BGP
sections.content:
A Flow Specification is a set of conditions describing packet traffic, such as source and destination prefixes, IP protocol and transport ports. A packet matches only when it meets every condition in the rule.

RFC 8955 encodes these rules as BGP Network Layer Reachability Information (NLRI) and defines BGP Extended Communities for actions to take on matching packets. It covers IPv4 unicast and IPv4 BGP/MPLS VPN services and describes use within or between providers.
sections.plainLanguage: A Flow Specification describes packet fields that a router should check. BGP distributes the rule and its associated action to routers that can process it.

sections.title: Encoding the Flow Specification
sections.content:
Peers use BGP multiprotocol attributes to advertise and withdraw Flow Specifications. IPv4 Flow Specification uses AFI 1 and SAFI 133; VPNv4 Flow Specification uses AFI 1 and SAFI 134. The next-hop length is zero and the next-hop address is ignored.

The NLRI begins with a length field followed by its components. Components must appear once each in increasing type order, and the rule matches the intersection of all included components. For VPNv4, an 8-octet Route Distinguisher precedes the same Flow Specification value.
sections.plainLanguage: The NLRI encodes the rule as an ordered list of packet fields. A packet must meet all listed conditions for the rule to match.

sections.title: Packet Fields and Comparison Operators
sections.content:
IPv4 component types cover destination and source prefixes, IP protocol, ports, ICMP type and code, TCP flags, packet length, DSCP and fragmentation. Numeric operators express comparisons such as equal, less than or greater than; bitmask operators compare selected bits.

Some components only apply when a packet has the relevant protocol header. For example, port components match TCP or UDP packets, and ICMP components match ICMP packets. A combination that cannot match any packet, such as an ICMP type together with a port, should not be propagated.
sections.plainLanguage: Rules can check addresses, protocol fields, ports, packet size and other header values. Comparison operators let a rule test for a value or range of values.

sections.title: Rule Ordering
sections.content:
Several Flow Specifications can match the same traffic, so routers need a consistent order that does not depend on the order in which BGP delivered the rules. The comparison begins with the lowest-numbered component type; when matching prefixes, the more-specific prefix takes precedence.

Other component values are compared as binary strings under the rules in the RFC. Terminal Action can let the filtering engine continue evaluating later rules, in which case actions from multiple matching rules are collected.
sections.plainLanguage: When several rules match, their component values determine which rule has precedence. This order stays independent of the order in which BGP delivered the rules.

sections.title: Validating Rules Against Unicast Routes
sections.content:
By default, an externally received Flow Specification must include a destination prefix. Its originator must match the originator of the best-match unicast route covering that prefix, and no more-specific unicast route may come from a different neighboring AS.

The router must also check that the left-most AS in an eBGP route's AS_PATH is the neighboring AS. It revalidates Flow Specifications when unicast routes change. Local configuration may relax the requirement for a destination prefix, in which case the related origin checks do not apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Before accepting an external rule, the router checks that its sender is associated with the unicast route to the destination. Changes to those routes require the router to check the rule again.

sections.title: Actions for Matching Traffic
sections.content:
With no filtering action attached, a matching packet follows the system's normal forwarding behavior. The RFC defines actions to limit bytes per second or packets per second, control whether later rules are evaluated, sample and log traffic, redirect traffic to a VRF, and change the packet's DSCP value.

A rate of zero means the matching traffic is discarded. All defined action communities are transitive. Several actions may apply to one rule, but actions can conflict; the implementation decides which conflicting actions to use and should document that behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: An action can limit, redirect, mark, sample or discard matching traffic. If two actions conflict, the implementation chooses how to handle them.

sections.title: VPN Distribution, Monitoring and Errors
sections.content:
VPN Flow Specifications are imported into VRFs according to Route Target matching and import policy. The rules apply only to traffic belonging to the VRFs where they are imported. The RFC also recommends facilities to log filtered packet headers and count matches for a rule.

Malformed Flow Specification data and malformed action communities are handled under the BGP error-handling procedures cited by the RFC. The VPN NLRI uses an 8-octet Route Distinguisher followed by the Flow Specification value.
sections.plainLanguage: VPN rules apply within the VRFs that import them. Routers can also log filtered headers and count how often a rule matches.

sections.title: Security and Changes from Earlier Rules
sections.content:
When validation ties rules to the matching unicast routes, the security properties are those of BGP unicast routing. Relaxing validation can allow unwanted filtering, marking or redirection, so the RFC calls for additional policy controls and capacity limits where needed.

RFC 8955 obsoletes RFC 5575 and RFC 7674. It clarifies component comparison rules, defines all action communities as transitive, adds a packet-rate action, incorporates redirect clarifications and adds error handling.
sections.plainLanguage: Validation and border policies help prevent unauthorized rules from changing traffic handling. This RFC replaces earlier Flow Specification rules and clarifies their encoding and actions.
